candidates.attacker_control: The UPDATE_GLOBAL_WHITE_ADDRS_CONFIG request header supplies both `aclFileFullPath` and `globalWhiteAddrs`; the broker passes them unmodified to AccessValidator.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig and then to PlainPermissionManager.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig (AdminBrokerProcessor lines 407-413). No server-side canonicalization or file-type validation is effective because of the inverted condition.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: A `startsWith(fileHome)` guard exists, but it is a raw string-prefix check with no path normalization, so it is both bypassable via `..` and overly broad for sibling paths sharing the prefix. The target must exist and must not be a directory (lines 486-490), and a target that fails YAML parsing (or throws in getYamlDataObject) aborts before writing (AclException propagates to the AdminBrokerProcessor catch at lines 426-431), which limits which files can be overwritten. The write runs as the broker user, so filesystem permissions bound the impact, and no command-execution sink is reachable from this path directly. The method is intended for admin tooling (tools UpdateGlobalWhiteAddrSubCommand passes a `.yml` path), which explains the existence of the check, but does not explain the inverted operator. No runtime test or build was executed; the decompiled/read behavior of FileWriter/rename is standard JDK semantics.
candidates.impact: Remote, targeted file overwrite (truncation and replacement) of any existing YAML-parseable file whose path string starts with rocketmq.home, executed with the broker process user's privileges; capability to rewrite ACL files, including the global whitelist, and thereby bypass ACL for attacker-chosen IPs (e.g. `*`) once the watcher reloads; corruption of unrelated configuration/data files under the RocketMQ home; and a functional denial for legitimate `.yaml` ACL files, which the inverted condition always rejects.
candidates.prerequisites: Network access to the broker remoting port (default 10911; 10909 fast port). With aclEnable=false (default, BrokerController.initialAcl lines 502-506), no credentials are required. With ACL enabled, the request code is not in Permission.ADMIN_CODE (acl/src/main/java/org/apache/rocketmq/acl/common/Permission.java lines 33-46), and checkPerm returns early because no resource-permission map is built for this code, so any authenticated non-admin account qualifies. The chosen target must already exist, not be a directory, share the unnormalized `fileHome` prefix, and parse as a YAML mapping (or be empty).
candidates.root_cause: In PlainPermissionManager.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig(List<String>, String) the guard at line 497 is `if (!fileName.endsWith(".yml") && fileName.endsWith(".yaml"))`. This is an incorrect negation: it rejects legitimate `.yaml` ACL files and accepts every other file name. The only other path restriction is a raw string-prefix check `fileName.startsWith(fileHome)` (line 492), with no normalization/real-path resolution, so `..` segments or a shared prefix are not caught. The function then parses the target as YAML and overwrites it via AclUtils.writeDataObject (new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(path))), so any existing non-directory file under the rocketmq.home string prefix that parses as a YAML mapping (empty files parse to null and are also accepted) is rewritten with attacker-influenced YAML content containing the caller-supplied globalWhiteRemoteAddresses list.
candidates.title: Inverted file-type validation in ACL global-white-address update allows targeted overwrite of non-ACL files under ROCKETMQ_HOME
candidates.trace: RequestCode.UPDATE_GLOBAL_WHITE_ADDRS_CONFIG (53) -> AdminBrokerProcessor.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig (lines 402-434) -> PlainAccessValidator.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig (lines 172-174) -> PlainPermissionManager.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig (lines 476-511): existence/directory check (486-490), raw prefix check (492-495), inverted suffix check (497-500) -> AclUtils.getYamlDataObject(fileName, Map.class) (AclUtils.java 235-257) -> map.put(AclConstants.CONFIG_GLOBAL_WHITE_ADDRS, globalWhiteAddrsList) (line 508) -> AclUtils.writeDataObject(fileName, ...) (AclUtils.java 259-275) -> FileWriter truncates/overwrites the target. For a `.yml` ACL target, AclFileWatchService reloads the file and PlainPermissionManager.load() installs the new global whitelist in memory; PlainPermissionManager.validate (lines 653-660) returns success for any client IP matching the global whitelist without signature or permission checks, i.e., an authentication/authorization bypass for the chosen IP.
candidates.unverified: Whether a given deployment exposes the broker port and has a suitable existing YAML-parseable file under rocketmq.home; exact upstream intended operator (the sibling code getAllAclFiles uses `endsWith(".yml") || endsWith(".yaml")`, and the log message says 'is not a ACL configuration file', both consistent with the intended check being `!(... || ...)`); no runtime confirmation of the ACL-reload bypass timing.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-73 External Control of File Name or Path; CWE-20 Improper Input Validation (also CWE-863 missing authorization on the same request path)

coverage_summary: The scope tool reports 875 model-visible files under the assigned root with no sensitive-name, size, symlink, or binary exclusions; the P1 relation index reports the same 875 files indexed (0 missing, 0 hash mismatches; 11,930 symbols, 28,271 edges, 373 facts), with no tests, build execution, SAST oracle, data-flow, or reachability proof. I read and traced the ACL stack (AclUtils, PlainPermissionManager, PlainAccessValidator, Permission, RemoteAddressStrategyFactory, PlainAccessResource), the namesrv request processor/controller, the broker AdminBrokerProcessor update/ACL handlers and BrokerController ACL wiring, remoting protocol decode/encode (NettyDecoder, RemotingCommand), and common Configuration/MixAll. The snapshot contains no test sources (the test module listed in pom.xml has no files), so no test-based corroboration exists.
limitations: No code, build, tests, or scanners were executed; all conclusions are static source reading, and no finding is runtime-confirmed.

Cannot diff against upstream or fixed revisions, so I could not prove which of the several plausible defects the snapshot was captured before; the chosen candidate is based on internal inconsistency and reachability only.
Only spot-checked store/CommitLog, client/MQClientAPIImpl, TLS, DLedger, filter, tools, and example modules; findings there would be additional to this review.

The P1 index is syntactic/navigational only (no control/data-flow or exploitability proof), and its facts carry no security verdict; index coverage of the file set is complete but does not substitute for semantic review of unread code.
Impact of the candidate depends on deployment details (broker port exposure, ACL setting, filesystem layout/permissions) that cannot be verified from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Unauthenticated configuration update on NameServer/Broker: DefaultRequestProcessor.updateConfig (namesrv, lines 557-590) and AdminBrokerProcessor.updateBrokerConfig (broker, lines 518-552) apply attacker-supplied Properties via Configuration.update (common Configuration.java 175-217) -> MixAll.properties2Object (MixAll.java 322-360). On the NameServer no ACL hook is ever registered (NamesrvController has no AccessValidator), and NamesrvConfig.configStorePath is used as the persist path (NamesrvController lines 69-73; Configuration.getStorePath 146-169; MixAll.string2File 146-180), so a single request can set configStorePath and write a properties file to an arbitrary path, with newline injection possible through Java properties `\n` escapes. This is the well-known RocketMQ updateConfig class and has high impact, but I did not select it as the candidate because it is the documented administrative API (docs/en/CLITools.md) whose safety rests on network isolation, and the snapshot's version window (4.9.6-SNAPSHOT) is more consistent with the ACL-path fix than with that CVE's fix; kept as an unconfirmed alternative lead.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible and high impact, but the source shows an intended admin API lacking a guard rather than an unambiguous defect; not selected to respect the one-candidate limit.

rejected_leads.lead: Privilege escalation through ACL-management requests: Permission.ADMIN_CODE (acl/.../Permission.java lines 33-46) omits UPDATE_AND_CREATE_ACL_CONFIG, DELETE_ACL_CONFIG and UPDATE_GLOBAL_WHITE_ADDRS_CONFIG, and PlainPermissionManager.checkPerm (lines 578-593) returns early when the request produces no resource-permission map. A valid non-admin ACL user could therefore create an admin account (AdminBrokerProcessor lines 325-365, request header admin=true) or whitelist itself, i.e., bypass ACL when aclEnable=true.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires ACL enabled plus a valid low-privileged credential, and I could not verify from the snapshot alone whether the omission is unintended (the docs only name UPDATE_AND_CREATE_TOPIC-style requests as admin). Left as an unconfirmed lead.

summary: Reviewed the RocketMQ 4.9.6-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (875 model-visible files, main sources only — no test module is present, and no code/build was executed). I traced security-relevant paths in acl, namesrv, broker processors, remoting protocol decode, and common configuration/MixAll. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is the broken validation in the ACL "global white address" update path (`PlainPermissionManager.updateGlobalWhiteAddrsConfig`), which lets a remote caller steer the update into non-ACL files and mis-rejects legitimate `.yaml` ACL files. Stronger-impact-but-less-crisp leads (unauthenticated UPDATE_NAMESRV_CONFIG/UPDATE_BROKER_CONFIG property update, and missing admin codes for ACL management requests) are recorded as rejected/unconfirmed leads, not as additional candidates.
